title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
text:
Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar.

From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme.

It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them.

It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time , which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross".

There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom.

Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96.

The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK.

Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones.

Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable.

"At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices.

"There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe."

She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time.

Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date.

"Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said.

The Retail Motor Industry Federation, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying.

Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year.

title: Colnago Bets Against the Massive Tire Trend With the Stretched G5-X
author: Josh Ross
text:
Today, the Colnago G5-X launches with a unique twist on a modern gravel race bike, marking a massive departure from the previous generation. The G4-X still had a foot on the cyclocross course and carried a road-esque feel. Ride it in 2026, and it feels like the perfect all-road bike with its 45mm max tire clearance. This time around, Colnago is looking at the challenge of off-road riding through a brand-new lens.

At this point in the history of gravel bikes, a new split has formed. While once there were gravel adventure bikes and gravel race bikes, now we’ve coalesced into a space where everything is both, and the choice comes down to short and steep geometry vs. long, low, and stable geometry.

The previous version of the bike fell into the road-like short and steep geometry, but this time around Colnago is firmly planting its flag in the long, low, and stable camp.

To understand the shift, you have to look at the bottom bracket. The G4-X utilized a 70mm drop, which kept the handling tight but perched the rider relatively high, much like a cyclocross frame. On the G5-X, Colnago increased that drop to 80mm on the smaller sizes and 77.5mm on the larger frames. In some ways this is about tire clearance, but that’s not the whole story. By dropping the bottom bracket nearly a full centimeter, the frame pulls your center of mass down, giving you an “in-the-bike” feel that should help with high-speed stability on loose surfaces.

The brand didn’t stop at the bottom bracket to achieve this composure. Colnago stretched the chainstays from 430mm to 435mm and slackened the head tube angle by half a degree down to 71.0° on the mid-sizes. This pushes the front wheel further out and lengthens the overall wheelbase. The geometry no longer demands constant, twitchy steering corrections. Instead, it is designed to self-center and track straight through washboard gravel and rutted descents without deflecting. The idea is to trade some of the snappy, tight-corner acceleration (which can be nervous depending on the use case) for predictability during ultra-endurance races like Badlands, which Colnago specifically mentioned.

What’s perhaps even more interesting is that these changes don’t come at the expense of fit. The upper part of the geometry, including stack, reach, and seat tube angles, remains almost the same. Clearly, the idea is to create the feel of a race bike while adding stability for rough and fast descents during a race.

The one place where we are not seeing much deviation from the norm is when it comes to tire clearance. The standard that seems to be emerging is 57mm, with 50mm being the bare minimum for a modern gravel bike.

The G4-X was a bike that stayed conservative with a max 45mm tire clearance. The update does bring a huge 8mm more clearance, but do the math there. Colnago is launching the latest G5-X with a max clearance of 53mm in a world where many of the fastest gravel race bikes are going quite a bit bigger.

While 53mm is conservative compared to the broader market, it is also a risk. Colnago is essentially drawing a line in the sand, betting that pushing clearance out to 57mm isn’t worth the compromises that come with it. Bigger tires tend to dominate the feel of a bike, and not always for the best. It would seem that Colnago considers 53mm big enough. On the upside, there are no stated limitations for 2x compatibility within that 53mm of clearance, and the max chainring size is 50t.

The musings about tire clearance are not actually supported by Colnago’s marketing, so it’s not exactly clear why this bike tops out at 53mm of clearance. Another possible reason is that Colnago chose to focus this bike around a series of American-style gravel races all around the world. It would seem that doing the calculations with The Traka, Unbound Gravel, Badlands, and GranGuanche Audax in mind, Colnago thinks 53mm is enough.

Part of those calculations, though, is that you need to carry things. Unlike the G4-X, the G5-X has integrated downtube storage. On top of that, there are the external mounting points to support the ultra-endurance races on that list. The bike features standard top tube mounts for a bento box (with a cover just like the G4-X), plus new mounts positioned under the downtube and on the fork legs. Colnago specifically added these to address the realities of events like Badlands and GranGuanche Audax, where sleeping out is unavoidable and riders need the ability to haul extra cargo, sleeping gear, and heavy water loads over multi-day stretches.

Another interesting choice is that every G5-X ships with three Fidlock Twist mounts. While it is still possible to use standard bottle cages, anyone who’s ever dealt with frame bags will understand the necessity of managing bottles packed into what space is left. The Fidlock design makes getting bottles in and out easier from the side while also eliminating bottle ejections on rough surfaces. The other advantage to Fidlock is more choice for carrying things. The third mount under the downtube might be a good choice for mounting tool cases or storage pods that can also take advantage of the magnetic mounts.

The last detail Colnago added with these races in mind is a switch from the previous D-shaped post to a new round 27.2mm seatpost. One aspect of this is the desire to add compliance through flex in the post, but Colnago also states that it is to allow more choice. Keep it rigid and choose whatever brand you want to fine-tune the flex, or swap to a dropper post for the roughest races.

The Colnago G5-X is available today worldwide. Find more info at the Colnago website .

title: China’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over?
author: Danny Vincent in Hong Kong
text:
Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents

G rowing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory.

“The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s.

By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets of China and beyond.

But now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuel China’s economic success are facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over.

Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on.

Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology.

“Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.”

“The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave.

“We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.”

According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation.

Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm.

“I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong.

His family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business.

“Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says.

According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of the country’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP . Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing.

Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth.

“The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says.

For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn.

“I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says.

“If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.”

Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

title: How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada
text:
For Alberta independence supporter Keith Wilson, the western Canadian province is in a league of its own.

With its wealth of rich oil and gas reserves, a significant agricultural sector and a young and skilled workforce, its economy is one to be reckoned with, says Wilson.

The province will hold a referendum on 19 October, giving residents two options: vote to stay in Canada, or vote to move ahead with a formal binding referendum on independence at a later date.

The vote, despite not being a cut and dry "stay or leave", still stands to be among the most consequential in recent Canadian history, and a significant test of national unity.

One key issue has become central to the debate: Would Alberta be richer if it were to become an independent country?

"Alberta's economy is unique. is fundamentally different than the rest of Canada's - we have the people, the institutions, the infrastructure to excel," he says.

Alberta separatists have long argued that the province has been short-changed by being part of Canada, and that more of the oil and gas wealth would be kept within its borders instead of being shared with Ottawa, delivering it tens of billions in savings.

But many disagree with their accounting.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposes independence, predicts a more sober outcome. She says the province could risk paying C$400bn ($283bn; £213bn) in transition costs alone, while bleeding billions more in lost investments and trade due to the political upheaval.

A report commissioned , external by her government released earlier this month calculated the costs of separation as between C$50bn and C$170bn over five years - and a highly unpredictable outlook over the long term.

The report cautions that the to-do list for a newly independent Alberta would be long and costly.

It would have to set up agencies to manage taxes and national security, develop its own constitution, legal and court systems, and pension plans, and negotiate the division of federal assets like national parks and military bases.

At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation

Alberta will vote on whether to remain part of Canada. What now?

Lennie Kaplan, a former finance official in Alberta, says the province would be expected to take on a share of Canada's national debt, among many other fiscal challenges and responsibilities.

A report on Alberta independence by the CanadaWest Foundation , external , a non-profit Alberta-based think tank, estimates that the province could be stuck with additional debt ranging from C$258bn to C$333bn.

With a projected hit to Alberta's GDP and the additional costs, the report estimates separation could hit Albertans' bottom line and reduce their disposable income by 5.8% on average.

"Why do we have to create all this uncertainty that might impact and impair the province's fiscal position going forward? Why wouldn't we just work within Canada to address these issues?" Kaplan asks.

Opinion polling indicates that around 20% to 25% of Albertans plan to vote in favour of moving ahead with a binding separation referendum, with higher support among younger, rural and conservative voters.

Behind the separatist push is the belief that Alberta is misunderstood and overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa. For decades, that sentiment fuelled a sense of "western alienation" in the prairie province.

Once a fringe movement, a number of factors pushed it to the forefront of Alberta politics.

There was anger over environmental and political pushback that killed proposed pipelines from landlocked Alberta to coastal waters.

A decade of Liberal government in Ottawa has also caused frustration in reliably conservative Alberta. And, in addition, there is also leftover distrust of the federal government over what some Albertans saw as excessive lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Over the past year, separatist organisers held townhalls across the province to gauge interest from the public. They then launched a citizen-led petition to separate earlier this year, which got more than 300,000 signatures.

Smith, the premier, decided earlier this year she would authorise a vote.

Alberta is home to Canada's oil and gas sector, with oil reserves estimated to be the fourth-largest in the world. Crude oil is by far Canada's most profitable commodity, accounting for C$142bn in export value in 2025 alone.

Most of it is sold to refineries in the US.

The province has the highest GDP per capita in the country, and it contributes billions a year to the federal tax pool because of its strong economy.

It has not received any "equalisation" payments - money that so-called "have not", or less wealthy, provinces receive from the federal government - since 1965.

Calculations by Tegan Hill and Nathaniel Li, economists at the Fraser Institute think tank, show that Alberta's total net contribution to Ottawa since 2007 has been C$322bn, or an average of around $17bn per year.

"That's nearly four times that of British Columbia, more than four times Ontario," Hill tells the BBC. "The other seven provinces were net recipients, meaning Ottawa spent or transferred more money to those provinces than it collected."

Hill explains that the amount Alberta contributes to the rest of Canada is one of the main frustrations cited by those in favour of separation.

The sentiment, she says, is that: "We're paying to support these other provinces, and if we just went our own way, we could keep all that wealth for ourselves."

This belief is at the heart of the economic projections from the Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the main groups organising in favour of independence.

In its fiscal plan, released last year , external , they estimate Alberta will save up to C$47bn annually if it stops paying federal taxes.…

title: The wildlife winners set to appear on your banknotes revealed
text:
Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.

The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.

The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.

Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.

"We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier.

A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations . Respondents were invited to select up to six.

More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes.

The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba).

The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category.

The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal.

The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline.

The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively .

Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes.

Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years.

He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch.

"We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said.

Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland , external .

Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history.

On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing.

The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do".

The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time.

title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
text:
The UK needs to do more back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.

Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.

Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market , are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.

The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.

"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss podcast .

The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.

Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.

But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.

Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.

Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns.

"We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.

There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.

But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said.

"We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit."

Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia Hoggett

The boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list.

However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.

She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax , external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.

She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.

Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.

It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.

The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month.

"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

title: Magnus Sheffield Embraces Norwegian Roots With Move to Uno-X
author: ahood
text:
Magnus Sheffield, shown here at the 2025 Paris-Nice, joins Uno-X on a four-year deal. (Photo: DAVID PINTENS/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images))

Magnus Sheffield is heading to Uno-X Mobility in a blockbuster move that brings the American all-rounder a little closer to home.

New York raised, yes. But Sheffield’s Norwegian roots run much deeper than his first name.

“Joining Uno-X Mobility feels like closing the circle on the journey my mum started when she moved to the US at 20. Uno-X has always been a team I was interested in, even before I became a professional,” Sheffield said in Wednesday’s announcement. “It was never a question of if, only when.”

The 24-year-old holds both American and Norwegian passports, grew up speaking Norwegian at home, and has family scattered around Oslo.

Now he’ll be racing with Uno-X through 2030.

Sheffield will be the first American to race on the team and first rider who isn’t Norwegian or Danish since its pro-level arrival in 2020.

Sheffield will leave Netcompany-Ineos after five seasons, having stepped up from Rally Cycling in 2022.

A New Yorker by birth, he won Brabantse Pijl at 19 during his first spring with the British team.

A Paris-Nice stage victory in 2025 and sixth at the 2024 Tour of Flanders are other hints of why Uno-X signed him to a multi-year deal.

General manager Thor Hushovd thinks there’s plenty left in the tank.

“Magnus is a rider with enormous potential, and I don’t think we have seen the full extent of it yet,” Hushovd said. “He has already finished fourth in Paris-Nice and sixth in Flanders. That tells you a lot about the range he has.”

For Uno-X, which stepped into the WorldTour in 2026, Sheffield’s four-year deal is the next big move of his career.

“This is one of the big signings for us, and one we are very proud of,” Hushovd said. “We believe we can give him the environment to take another step and develop into one of the leading riders in the sport.”

Sheffield joins an incoming group that includes Casper Pedersen (Soudal Quick-Step), Felix Ørn-Kristoff (Lotto Intermarché), and Kristian Egholm from (Lidl-Trek Future Racing) — all Danes and Norwegians, of course.

Maybe call him half-Norwegian. His deep family ties to Norway help explain why both sides see this as such a good fit.

“Language is an important part of the identity we have built as a team. Magnus understands the culture and can become part of it naturally from day one,” Hushovd said. “And on top of everything he can do on the bike, he is an incredibly good guy.”

And speaking Norwegian in team meetings?

That won’t be a problem. He already speaks it fluently.

“My mum grew up in Gjøvik, and most of our family now lives around Oslo. She moved to the U.S. to study when she was 20, and that’s where she met my dad,” he said. “We always spoke Norwegian at home. It was almost our secret family language growing up in the U.S.”

Family visits and Norwegian traditions were part of Sheffield’s childhood long before cycling became his day job.

His sister now lives in Norway, and his brother spent several years there before returning to the United States to study.

Now he’s bringing that connection into the WorldTour.

title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart
author: Heather Stewart Economics editor
text:
The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy

Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election.

In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass.

But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early.

So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it.

The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall , underlined how unpopular it is.

But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be.

The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24.

And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax.

Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain.

Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return.

Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that.

Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC .

The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move.

And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available.

As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive.

He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said.

Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax.

If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.

title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley
author: Nils Pratley
text:
Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills

South West Water owner taps investors after sewage spills

W ater is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week , reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England.

And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride.

But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances).

Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures.

The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place.

Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”.

Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism.

The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low.

For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine.

One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point.

If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper.

Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I heard that all summer’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
As we patiently wait for the Knicks to host the Wiz Kiz on Thursday…

…here are the latest quotables from around Tarrytown and elsewhere.

On the Knicks’ lack of physicality against Philadelphia:

“What bothers me is our lack of physicality throughout the ball game, and that’s the whole roster up and down. We weren’t great on the ball physically and we weren’t great with our defensive positioning physically.

“The rest of the [issues are] coach talk. It’s real, but it’s coach talk that we’ll clean up watching film and all that stuff. I can’t help with the physicality. That they’ve gotta find individually, which will then turn into collectively, and that’s how you find minutes. That’s how you make the team. That’s how you contribute in a way where some of those other mistakes can be ‘OK, we’ll get better in that area and we’ll get better in this area.’

“But the physicality, we have to do a better job of that from top to bottom.”

On the Knicks making the game easy for the 76ers:

“They got to wherever they wanted to when it comes to getting to their spots and getting good shots. We didn’t contest, we didn’t rear-view challenge and we made the game easy for them. We just turned and took a step to the rim and they came right over our back and got the offensive rebound, so that I’m concerned about and I don’t want to see happen.”

On the Knicks’ poor 3-point shot selection:

“I don’t care if we go 0 for 40. We took 41 and 33 of those [threes] weren’t sprays. And that’s not how we play.”

On the importance of the Knicks’ preseason opener:

“[I put] a good amount [of stock in this preseason game]. Obviously being results-based is not necessarily a focus, but it’s like process-driven and making sure the details are there and doing all the right things. I think those are the things you need to be concerned about, results-based not so much. Obviously we want to win but make sure the process is right.”

On the second apron being used as an excuse by teams when navigating free

“I heard that all summer.”

On being surprised by his diminished free-agent market:

“I was very surprised. I played every single game last year, played meaningful minutes the whole year. Thought I did decently or good enough in my role that I was given. But when free agency started, that wasn’t the case.”

On proving himself while competing for a Knicks roster spot:

“You got to prove yourself every year. I’ve been on eight teams in nine years. Every year you got to prove yourself, prove you’ve gotten better. But with this team obviously the first and second units are pretty set, I’d say. So obviously I’d have to provide a winning attitude. I’m fighting for a job right now. So any role they give me, I’d be happy to do it.”

On returning to New York after previously playing for the Nets during the KD era:

“I love New York. Obviously playing in Brooklyn, they’re little brother to the Knicks even if, at the time, they weren’t that good and we were really good. New York’s always a place I loved, loved winning, loved being around. When I got the call, I was like, ‘Yeah, for sure.’ ”

On wanting to play for a contender:

“As you know, at this point in my career, only contending teams look for me. So I’m just trying to compete for a championship. Go back to back and help them win again.”

On fighting for a guaranteed roster spot:

“It is what it is right now. I thought I played well enough last year to be in the running for a guaranteed job. But now I just got to show my work throughout the summer and my veteran leadership somehow.”

On seeing the 76ers as a threat to the Knicks:

“The Sixers can make a title run. The Sixers are the team to watch out for if you’re the New York Knicks. To me, it’s clearly about the Knicks and the Philadelphia 76ers.”

On James Dolan and the lack of extensions for Leon Rose and William Wesley:

“Let me put everybody in New York on blast. That damn James Dolan is getting in the way again. We have some concerns. First of all, I don’t know if it’s news or not. Where the hell is the extension for Leon Rose? Where the hell is the extension for Worldwide Wes, William Wesley? Worldwide Wes and Leon Rose ended a 53-year drought and brought a championship to New York. Where’s their extension? Where is it? That’s number one.”

On the Knicks’ current contract offer to Karl-Anthony Towns:

“Number two, I’m not going to tell you that Karl-Anthony Towns deserves the max. I understand that you got Brunson and Anunoby coming down the pike, but you don’t disrespect that man by cutting him short by $77 million. You don’t do that. You give him a respectable offer.”

“You give him an offer that says, ‘Okay, listen. We need you to take this hit. Jalen Brunson took this hit. We need you to do it, too.’ So, it ain’t $277 million. It might be $225-$227 million, something along those lines because Brunson took a hit, too.”

“You might not like it, but it’s not disrespectful. You’re saying, ‘Listen, I got the cats that you want to keep with you. I’m going to have to touch that second apron. I’m going to have to take care of your other cats.’”

On the Knicks needing to take care of Jalen Brunson first:

“And we know you got to, to use his term, Big Body Brunson. We got to take care of him. That’s what we can’t go to Brunson and ask him to take another cut. The man delivered the chip, and he was the superstar that did it. Okay, he is the franchise. There will be a statue erected outside of Madison Square Garden for that man one day. He erased a 53-year drought.”

“Okay, we got to take care of Brunson. So, we might need y’all to take some hits, but you don’t disrespect him.”

On the Knicks’ history and Towns’ value to the championship team:

“For 53 years, the New York Knicks didn’t do anything but pass gas and try to tell us it was perfume. That’s what they did. They stunk up the joint year after year after year, and they finally won the chip.”

“Karl-Anthony Towns has everything to do with that. I’m not telling you that he ain’t worth—first of all, he’s worth the $277 million in today’s NBA economy. It’s just that, in light of other people you have to take care of, it’s going to call for some level of sacrifice.”

“But you don’t disrespect him. Karl-Anthony Towns deserves more money, and most importantly, he deserves to be respected and appreciated. And I’mma tell you why: New York has a problem.”

On his concerns about James Dolan after the Knicks’ championship:

“They got a problem because that same damn James Dolan that stunk up the joint for years running the New York Knicks franchise finally, after 27 years at the helm, won a chip.”

“It wouldn’t surprise me at all if his mentality is, ‘All right, I delivered a chip. So now we can wait another quarter century before we win it again.’ He’s the kind of person that’ll have that kind of attitude and take that for granted.”

On what he sees as a broader problem with Knicks ownership:

“I’m speaking to a bigger problem. I’m speaking to a level of arrogance and dismissiveness on the part of the ownership that’s focused on the fact that he’s a champion now and not really reflecting on the years of ineptitude that he exercised running this franchise.”

“And if Karl-Anthony Towns isn’t taken care of, it sends the wrong message: ‘we don’t necessarily take care of our own.’ You see what I’m saying? And that’s where it’ll lead to you not winning for the next quarter-century and beyond when you ignore your own.”

“Even when the Lakers struggled, the Buss family always took care of the people who took care of them. That is what James Dolan has to remember.

“Leon Rose deserves his money. Worldwide Wes deserves his money. Brunson and Anunoby deserve their money. Karl-Anthony Towns deserves the money. They clearly made money for James Dolan this past season. Yeah, they made money for him. Let’s be clear.”

title: ‘Risk Your Life To Race’: Wrong-Way Police Motorbike Hits Pidcock’s Teammates
author: ahood
text:
Pidcock almost quit the race in anger. (Photo: Getty Images/Instagram)

Tom Pidcock nearly quit Tuesday’s Tre Valli Varesine in a fury after a police motorbike traveling against the race struck two of his teammates.

Marcel Camprubí and Thomas Gloag went down in the collision before live television coverage began.

Camprubí continued, but Gloag abandoned and needed stitches in his knee, according to Pidcock and Pinarello-Q36.5 officials.

“A police motorbike was going the wrong way down the course and crashed into two of our guys,” Pidcock told CyclingProNet after the finish.

“I wanted to stop the race afterwards, or at least withdraw myself, because I was absolutely furious.”

Pidcock eventually finished second behind Jarno Widar.

Camprubí later posted a photograph of his wrecked bike, its front fork snapped through.

“It is sad that you have to risk your life to race, one month after a tragic accident,” he wrote on Instagram .

Another day in Italy, another safety scare in pro racing.

The incident followed a bruising Monday at Coppa Bernocchi .

Andrea Raccagni fractured a neck vertebra and Alex Aranburu broke his collarbone and part of his pelvis in the pileup about 600 meters from the finish.

Marijn van den Berg was relegated off the podium following a race jury decision.

Earlier in the race, a DHL delivery van pulled onto the course with about 19km remaining, slotting between the breakaway and the chase. Race organizers later apologized for the safety slip-up.

Cycling’s safety debate has been simmering in the background for years.

The latest tragedy came when Finlay Tarling, 19, died at the Volta a Portugal after a collision involving a non-race vehicle in August, according to reporting citing local authorities.

Keeping vehicles off race courses should be among the basics, Pidcock said.

“This simply must not happen,” Pidcock said.

title: Il Lombardia 2026 Cheat Sheet: Route, Climbs, Favorites, Storylines for Final Monument of 2026
author: ahood
text:
Simmons, shown last year with fourth, is one of the top names for Il Lombardia. (Photo: Sara Cavallini/Getty Images)

The leaves are falling, the season is fading, and cycling’s final monument is wide open at this weekend’s Il Lombardia .

Brandon McNulty , Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas , and Isaac del Toro headline the contenders for Il Lombardia on October 10.

With five-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar sidelined with injury, the elite men’s road season’s final big date will see a peloton keen to fill the void.

For the first time since 2020, somebody with the last name other than Pogačar will lift the trophy.

Will that make it a better race? We’re about to find out.

The Slovenian’s absence could give Evenepoel a chance to win his first Lombardia victory. He’ll square off with recently crowned world champion McNulty and a deep field of favorites.

Nobody gets an easy ride going into the offseason. Il Lombardia is the last real hit-out in what’s been a wild and thrilling 2026 road season.

The 120th edition packs 239km and 4,600m of climbing between Bergamo and Como, with the Ghisallo, Civiglio, and two trips up San Fermo della Battaglia waiting to squeeze out whatever juice the legs might have left.

Here’s everything you need to know about the 2026 “Race of the Falling Leaves,” aka Il Lombardia.

Date : Saturday, October 10 Edition : 120th Start : Bergamo, Italy Finish : Como, Italy Distance : 239km Elevation gain : 4,600m Climbs : Nine, counting the early Bocche di Gavarno rise Start : 10:45 a.m. CET Expected finish : 4:40 to 5:20 p.m. CET Defending champion : Tadej Pogačar, sidelined with injury Nickname : Race of the Falling Leaves

Il Lombardia switches direction for 2026, starting in Bergamo and finishing in Como after the reverse route in 2025.

That matters because the Como finish brings the steep Civiglio climb and its twisting descent into the late-race equation, followed by one final haul over San Fermo della Battaglia.

The opening climbs around Bergamo give the breakaway room to move and the peloton plenty of opportunity to settle in for a long day.

The route then crosses Brianza, drops toward Lecco, and follows Lake Como to Bellagio for the ascent of the Madonna del Ghisallo.

From there, the race heads toward Como and a finale built around San Fermo, Civiglio, and San Fermo again.

The course rolls out from Bergamo and opens with Bocche di Gavarno, Selvino, Colle di Berbenno, and Valpiana before reaching the sharper climbs toward Como. The early breaks will move and the chase is on.

Giovenzana adds a new challenge with about 100km remaining. The 3.6km ascent averages 9.2 percent, with a 750-meter section at 14 percent and ramps reaching 16 percent.

The iconic Madonna del Ghisallo hits out above Bellagio, climbing 8.6km at 6.2 percent to the iconic sanctuary overlooking Lake Como.

The final circuit packs Civiglio between two ascents of San Fermo della Battaglia. Civiglio climbs 4.2km at 9.7 percent, with a narrow road and a twisting descent that sprung Vincenzo Nibali to victory in 2015 and 2017.

San Fermo bites at 2.7km at 7.2 percent. Its second ascent is the final climb, topping out at about 5km from the finish before a fast descent into Como and a flat final kilometer.

Action guaranteed until the end. The tifosi will be out in droves.

Just like when he’s in a race, Pogačar’s absence also changes the entire conversation.

A Pog-free Lombardia is one without the overwhelming defending favorite to dictate how everybody else races.

Several teams start with more than one potential winner in what should be a wide-open race.

Evenepoel, McNulty, and an on-form and angry Ciccone top the list, with Seixas, Del Toro, Juan Ayuso, Matteo Jorgenson, Quinn Simmons , and Tom Pidcock among the other top names on the provisional start list.

Remco Evenepoel: His best Lombardia chance yet

Evenepoel arrives coming off his spectacular European championship bike-throw, and he’s been runner-up in the past two editions of Lombardia.

He already owns two Liège-Bastogne-Liège titles, so winning Saturday would give him a third monument victory and his first at Lombardia.

Without Pogačar, the Belgian becomes the five-star favorite. Rivals won’t want to give him any daylight, especially anywhere on the final circuit.

Brandon McNulty : Rainbow jersey, monument dreams

McNulty brings the world champion’s jersey into a race no American has won.

His Montréal victory confirmed his potential on long, attritional races. A strong week in his rainbow jersey debut bodes well for a big ride this weekend.

UAE also brings del Toro, giving the superteam another attacking option as it tries to keep the trophy in-house.

Giulio Ciccone and Juan Ayuso : Two cards for Lidl-Trek

Ciccone heads to Lombardia after his agonizing photo finish defeat to Evenepoel at the European championships.

The steep Como finale suits his climbing strengths, and racing on home roads adds another incentive to try to become Italy’s first winner since Nibali’s second in 2017.

Alongside Ayuso, Lidl-Trek packs two riders capable of playing the odds.

Simmons — who rode a monster race last year to finish fourth — is also confirmed for Lidl-Trek.

Seixas and del Toro won’t be content to follow the wheels.

Both have the climbing legs to go deep into the race, and both are chasing redemption after the Montréal worlds.

The tactical question is whether they will hide in the bunch until the final climbs or force the selection themselves early.

For either one to win, they’ll have to get past each other. Neither has won a monument yet. This could be their best chance.

Matteo Jorgenson, Tom Pidcock : The other contenders

Jorgenson and Pidcock both showed top form at Tre Valli, even if Jarno Widar outplayed them in the final sprint.

Davide Piganzoli, Giulio Pellizzari, and Antonio Tiberi add to the Italian options. Ben Healy is always a name to watch in any climb-heavy race.…

title: Russell to start from back of Singapore grid after penalty
text:
Britain's George Russell will start from the back of the grid in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver has received a power-unit penalty from a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday.

The 28-year-old qualified in eighth but was heading for a podium finish before an engine failure forced him to retire from third place with five laps remaining.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has confirmed that Russell needs to take a new power unit this weekend, putting him over the limit on several components and meaning he will be penalised in Singapore.

Russell's retirement last Sunday meant Kimi Antonelli, who finished second behind Max Verstappen, took a big leap towards his first Formula 1 world title as the Italian is now 84 points ahead of his Mercedes team-mate.

There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs for Qatar and Abu Dhabi, in the context of the war in the Middle East.

"[Russell's penalty] is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for," said Wolff.

"Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."

The engine penalty is a particularly large blow for Russell as overtaking is notoriously difficult in Singapore.

His title hopes are already effectively over with either six or seven races still o go, even if he still has a mathematical chance of catching Antonelli.

But it means his chances of cutting the Italian’s lead are drastically reduced, even if Antonelli runs into trouble.

Mercedes had no choice but to fit a new engine for Russell in Singapore because he had no usable engines remaining in his allocation.

After early season reliability problems, they were all either broken or too high on mileage.

Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix last month having taken a similar penalty, while this is the latest setback in a season of frustrating mechanical issues for Russell, who won last year's Singapore Grand Prix.

Extra points are on offer this weekend as Singapore hosts the sixth and final sprint event of the season. Russell's penalty will apply to Sunday's Grand Prix and not the sprint race on Saturday.

"We have spent the days since [last Sunday] working hard to understand why our performance was not where it should have been," Wolff added.

"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work.

"We need to keep learning and score the strongest result we can with both cars."

title: Pogačar’s Viral Booty Band Warm-Up Routine Might Just Be a Placebo, but Here’s Why It Might Work for You
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Tadej Pogačar made “booty bands” everybody’s favorite warm-up ritual when he was filmed twerking and squatting his way through a pre-race routine, bands around his knees.

But it turns out that these wildly popular pre-ride workouts might largely be a placebo .

Waddling, lunging, and squatting through a mini-band session before a ride doesn’t “activate your glutes” or prime you to push max power.

According to WorldTour experts, the power of glute bands might largely be in the mind.

“These mini band moves are beneficial, but it’s more from a pseudo-science perspective. Someone riders might feel like, ‘Oh, I’m doing something , I’m preparing myself to ride’ by doing them,” Jayco-AlUla physiotherapist Dan Guillemette told Velo .

“But in terms of actual performance, it’s really unlikely there’s any actual benefit.”

So how have mini-bands become one of sport’s most popular primers?

They’ve become no-brainers for WorldTour and triathlon pros, TikTok influencers, 4w/kg Velo writers [ ahem ], and everyone in between.

Here’s why mini band warm-ups might not be worth your time – unless you’re already doing them – and how to make better use of these wildly popular home workout tools.

Pogačar’s pre-race warm-up video was one of the viral cycling clips of 2025. The meme pages loved it.

The Instagram reel shows Pogačar and his teammate Juan Molano working through a series of mini band exercises ahead of a stage at the UAE Tour. Pogi’s now-famous “bum to the sky” hip opener was a particular highlight.

It was a rare behind-the-scenes glimpse at how pros prepare to push wild watts for hours on end.

Since then, clips of Matteo Jorgenson , Jonas Abrahamsen , and Remco Evenepoel doing similar routines have reinforced the thinking that a few minutes inside a mini band will push you to new performance peaks.

And unlike a set of Pogačar-approved 165mm cranks or an indoor trainer “heat suit,” there’s no expensive equipment, excess sweat, or annoying apps involved.

All you need is a $10 band from Walmart and one of the routines being pumped into your cycling social feed.

The big selling point of booty band routines for cyclists and endurance athletes?

That they waken your glutes from their slumber after too long being sat on. A few minutes pushing at a mini band will buzz your butt into “workout mode.”

Strength expert Chris Peden burst that bubble when he spoke to Velo .

Peden, the head of S&C at Decathlon CMA-CGM, said pros and amateurs alike have been fooled by a misapplication of the term “sleepy glutes.”

“These routines are always advertised as ‘you’ve got weak glutes, your glutes don’t work, or are ‘asleep.’ That’s the result of medical terms transferring to the performance world that don’t really apply,” Peden told Velo . “It’s a medical term from those who are extremely inactive, not somebody who does even a low level of training.

“And anyway, muscles don’t ‘switch on’ or ‘switch off,’” Peden continued. “Your neuromuscular system is always working. Your brain knows exactly what to recruit at any one time,” Peden said.

“A band workout does not make that signal ‘better’ or ‘cleaner,’ as some suggest. It’s unlikely to have any benefit at all.”

If you’re reading this post, you’re likely interested in bikes and maybe ride one every so often.

A second misconception? That squeezing some torque out of your glutes with an oversized elastic band will ready you for your 400-watt interval workout.

That’s founded in another misapplication, this time of the term “PAP.”

PAP, or Post Activation Potentiation, refers to the acute boost in muscular performance following a previous activity. A set of heavy back squats before attempting a maximum vertical jump is a common real-world application of PAP.

But sadly, a set of waddling “monster walks” won’t come close to delivering the muscular force or speed required for any meaningful PAP.

In the world’s biggest bike races, turbo trainers – not mini bands – are used to provide an effective potentiation.

These torture devices are wheeled out of team trucks ahead of time trials, hard uphill starts, or for those wanting to make the day’s early break. Riders work through a progressive build before a series of short submaximal efforts that fully stimulate the muscles for a fast racing start.

So, wait one sec. If the popular theories behind booty bands are a load of BS, why are they still so popular in the dialed-down, scientifically-backed WorldTour?

Even Peden admitted his own athletes on Decathlon CMA-CGM do them, even though he dismisses their direct impact on performance. Both he and Guillemette at Jayco-AlUla think that for many riders, the gains are all in the mind.

For many, workout bands became part of their pre-ride routine as juniors, either as a misguided warm-up tool or as a minimal dose of strength work.

“Psychologically, the placebo effect is massive,” Peden said. “Our riders still do them regardless of what we might say. They’ve been told to do it since they were 15 years old, and that it’s beneficial to them. So I can’t turn around to tell them to suddenly stop.

“They’re not doing any harm, but they’re not achieving anything meaningful as a supposed ‘activation,’” he continued. “If they’re proving some psychological benefit and riders believe they help, I’m not going to hold them back. However, I might try to suggest they include some more useful practices, instead – say, around mobility.”

Guillemette, who worked at Team Sky before he joined Jayco-AlUla, added that a band routine can also help riders transition out of inactivity.

They prime the mind and loosen the body.

“It’s really unlikely that there’s any benefit to using bands in terms of race performance,” Guillemette said.…

title: Rainmakers: The drones used to seed clouds
text:
On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."
